subject: chemistry
title: pH, Kw and strong acids and bases
key_idea: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], so each pH unit is a tenfold change in [H⁺]. The ionic product of water, Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻], links [H⁺] and [OH⁻] and lets you find the pH of a strong base.

blocks.text: This section defines pH and shows how to convert between pH and [H⁺]. [H⁺] is the concentration of hydrogen ions in mol/dm³.

items.meaning: The negative logarithm to base 10 of the hydrogen ion concentration.
The concentration of hydrogen ions, in mol/dm³.

blocks.label: pH from hydrogen ion concentration
where: pH = the pH value, with no unit

items: [H⁺] covers a very wide range, so a logarithmic scale is used.
A change of one pH unit is a tenfold change in [H⁺]. Lower pH means higher [H⁺].
Under standard conditions, pure water has pH 7, acidic solutions have pH below 7 and alkaline solutions have pH above 7.

diagram.alt: A practice question comparing hydrogen ion concentrations at two pH values.
diagram.question: How many times greater is [H⁺] in a solution of pH {a} than in a solution of pH {b}?
working: Each pH unit is a factor of 10 in [H⁺].

items: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺] and [H⁺] = 10^(−pH).
One pH unit is a factor of 10 in [H⁺].
Water is pH 7 under standard conditions; acids are below and alkalis above.

blocks.text: A strong acid dissociates completely in water. This means [H⁺] equals the acid concentration for a monobasic acid.

items.text: [H⁺] = concentration of the acid. For a dibasic strong acid treated as fully dissociated, such as H₂SO₄, [H⁺] = 2 × concentration.
Give the pH to two decimal places, as the data allow.

items: To go the other way, [H⁺] = 10^(−pH). A pH of 2.40 gives [H⁺] = 4.0 × 10⁻³ mol/dm³.
Diluting a strong acid ten times raises its pH by exactly 1.
A strong acid is fully dissociated, so [H⁺] = [acid] for a monobasic acid.
Calculate pH with −log₁₀[H⁺].

sections.heading: The ionic product of water, Kw

blocks.text: Water is slightly dissociated. This section covers the equilibrium and what it means for strong bases.

items: Kw comes from the equilibrium constant for the dissociation of water. The concentration of water is constant and is included in Kw.
At 298 K, Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol²/dm⁶.
The value of Kw changes with temperature. Dissociation is endothermic, so Kw rises as temperature rises.
In pure water [H⁺] = [OH⁻], so the water is neutral at every temperature. At a higher temperature neutral pH is below 7.

blocks.text: The pH of a strong base

items.text: For NaOH, [OH⁻] equals the concentration of the base. For Ba(OH)₂, [OH⁻] = 2 × concentration.

items: Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] and is 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol²/dm⁶ at 298 K.
Kw increases with temperature.
For a strong base find [OH⁻], then [H⁺] = Kw ÷ [OH⁻], then pH.

checks.q: Calculate the pH of 0.0250 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid.
Calculate the pH of 0.0100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide at 298 K (Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol²/dm⁶).
Explain why pure water at 323 K, where Kw = 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol²/dm⁶, is neutral but has a pH below 7.
checks.a: [H⁺] = [OH⁻] so it is neutral. [H⁺] = √(5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 2.3 × 10⁻⁷ mol/dm³, so pH = 6.63, which is below 7.

extra.heading: Weak acids: Ka, pKa and pH

blocks.text: A weak acid is only partly dissociated, so [H⁺] is much less than the acid concentration. Its dissociation is an equilibrium with its own constant, Ka.

blocks.label: Acid dissociation constant
where: Ka = acid dissociation constant (mol/dm³ for a monobasic acid)

blocks.label: pKa
where: a smaller pKa means a stronger acid

items: In a solution of the acid alone, each HA that dissociates gives one H⁺ and one A⁻, so [H⁺] = [A⁻].
Very little acid dissociates, so [HA] at equilibrium is taken as the starting concentration.
Then Ka = [H⁺]² ÷ [HA], so [H⁺] = √(Ka × [HA]).
Ka changes only with temperature.

items.text: A 0.0500 mol/dm³ weak acid has pH 3.00, so [H⁺] = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol/dm³.

items: Ka = [H⁺][A⁻] ÷ [HA] and pKa = −log₁₀Ka.
For a weak acid, [H⁺] = √(Ka × [HA]).
Strong acids and alkalis use the full-dissociation working above.
